title: A Winter for the Visitor
premise: Rafael Oyelaran takes a teaching post in the snowbound village of Hollowmere, where a class of children vanished decades ago and the school still holds their desks. She discovers the missing students were lured by 'the Song,' a melody the frost itself sings each winter, and that her new house's mirrors are keeping time with something that isn't her reflection. The song has four verses; anyone who learns the last verse becomes its next voice, and the village elders have been feeding newcomers to it for generations to keep their own names off the frost. Rafael, who survived an earlier winter by staying silent and invisible, must finally choose between singing along to save herself or learning the last verse to unmake the song entirely—ending it at the cost of her own voice, which she gives willingly so the frozen children can finally go home.
about_author: Emrys Winterbourne is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who taught for six years in northern communities where winters isolate whole valleys for months. They write horror about institutions, silence, and the things people agree not to notice.

chapters.title: The Long Road In
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Rafael as the bus leaves her at Hollowmere's edge in early snow. The driver refuses to look at the school. Emotional beat: wary hope—she has spent twelve years perfecting invisibility, and this job feels like one more place to hide.

chapters.title: Twenty-Nine Empty Desks
chapters.summary: Rafael meets headmaster Corwin Hale, who shows her a classroom with twenty-nine extra desks no one will remove. POV: Rafael. Beat: unease dressed as bureaucracy; Hale's rehearsed answers about 'the consolidation.'

chapters.title: House on Fenwick Lane
chapters.summary: Rafael moves into her rented cottage and finds a child's chalk hopscotch grid scorched into the floorboards under the rug. POV: Rafael. Beat: the first private wrongness—the house remembers someone small.

chapters.title: The Class That Isn't
chapters.summary: Her first week teaching goes well until she counts attendance: thirty-one students enrolled, twenty-two present, and the register lists nine names no child claims. POV: Rafael. Beat: professional denial hardening into quiet investigation.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Remembers Nothing
chapters.summary: Rafael visits the village archivist, elderly Mrs. Aldous, who cheerfully insists no class ever went missing here. POV: Rafael. Beat: gaslight by kindness; the whole town performs normalcy like a chorus.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: At home, Rafael notices her mirror reflects her movements a beat behind. She tests it with a dropped cup; the reflection drops it late. POV: Rafael. Beat: terror arriving as arithmetic—something is watching through the glass.

chapters.title: What the Children Know
chapters.summary: A student, Idris Boone, draws the cottage's hopscotch grid from memory and says his gran told him never to step on it after dark. POV: Rafael. Beat: the first ally; the children carry what the adults buried.

chapters.title: The Frost Writes
chapters.summary: Overnight, ferns of frost bloom across Rafael's windows in patterns resembling musical notation. She photographs them; the photos show only blank glass. POV: Rafael. Beat: dread becoming intimate—the house is being written on.

chapters.title: Hale's Warning
chapters.summary: Headmaster Hale privately tells Rafael to keep her curtains drawn and never hum in the building. He won't say why. POV: Rafael. Beat: a frightened man offering rules instead of truth.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Noise
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: young Rafael surviving a bad winter in another town by staying silent through whatever moved in the walls, telling herself every noise had an explanation. POV: Rafael (past). Beat: reveals her survival strategy—and its cost.

chapters.title: The First Verse
chapters.summary: Idris's little sister sings two lines of an old skipping rhyme on the playground; all the birds leave the trees at once. POV: Rafael. Beat: the song is real, alive, and the children feed it without knowing.

chapters.title: Minutes of the Village Council
chapters.summary: Rafael breaks into the council archive and finds meeting minutes from 1971 recording a vote: 'the tithe'—one newcomer each winter. The signatures include Hale's father. POV: Rafael. Beat: justice theme ignites; the law here is the predator.

chapters.title: Reflections That Aren't Hers
chapters.summary: The mirrors now show the room as it was forty years ago—a child's bedroom, small shoes by the door. POV: Rafael. Beat: grief entering the horror; the house is haunted by absence, not malice.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Confesses
chapters.summary: Aldous, drunk, admits the village sings the first three verses every solstice to keep the frost fed, and that the last verse is known only to those already taken. POV: Rafael. Beat: complicity revealed; ordinary people chose survival over children.

chapters.title: The Tithe Is Chosen
chapters.summary: Rafael finds her own name written in frost on the school's back door. The council has selected her. POV: Rafael. Beat: invisibility fails—staying hidden was never an option.

chapters.title: Idris Follows the Music
chapters.summary: Idris goes missing overnight; searchers find his footprints ending neatly at the treeline, as if he simply stopped existing there. POV: Rafael. Beat: guilt detonates; her investigation drew the frost to him.

chapters.title: The Search
chapters.summary: Rafael searches the woods against Hale's orders and finds the old schoolhouse annex, boarded since 1971, humming faintly. POV: Rafael. Beat: resolve replacing fear; she crosses the threshold of the story's heart.

chapters.title: Inside the Annex
chapters.summary: In the annex, twenty-nine desks face a blackboard covered in the song's notation, and the air is warm despite the ruin. POV: Rafael. Beat: awe and violation—the song has a home, and it is institutional.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: Alone in the annex, Rafael involuntarily hears the second verse complete itself in her mind. She realizes knowledge is infection. POV: Rafael. Beat: contamination—learning is the trap.

chapters.title: Wax and Wool
chapters.summary: Rafael stuffs her ears with waxed wool and interrogates Aldous in writing, learning the third verse can be refused but the fourth cannot be unheard once heard. POV: Rafael. Beat: desperate pragmatism; she begins fighting on the song's terms.

chapters.title: Hale Breaks
chapters.summary: Hale confesses his family has supplied the tithe for three generations and begs Rafael to accept it quietly, promising her a good life until solstice. POV: Rafael. Beat: love-against-duty tension—he offers her survival at the village's price.

chapters.title: The Mirror Speaks
chapters.summary: The cottage mirror finally syncs perfectly—and the reflection is not Rafael but a small girl mouthing words: 'the last verse sets us free.' POV: Rafael. Beat: reversal; the haunting may be a plea, not a hunt.

chapters.title: Names in the Frost
chapters.summary: Rafael deciphers the window-frost notation: it is a ledger of names, each verse adding lines, the fourth verse reserved for the newest name. POV: Rafael. Beat: the pattern completes; the frost writes its final pattern only when the tithe accepts.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: The village gathers in the square to sing the first three verses; Rafael watches from the crowd, feeling the melody pull at her memory like a hook. POV: Rafael. Beat: communal menace; the whole town is the choir.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: When the congregation turns to Rafael to lead the response, she stays silent. The frost on every window in the square cracks at once. POV: Rafael. Beat: defiance—the cost of silence made public.

chapters.title: Taken
chapters.summary: That night the cold enters the cottage. Rafael wakes in the annex, unharmed, among the vanished children, who are neither dead nor alive but held mid-note. POV: Rafael. Beat: crossing fully into the other side of the song.

chapters.title: The Children of 1971
chapters.summary: The taken children tell her their side: they heard the last verse and could not stop singing it, and they have been the song's voice ever since. POV: Rafael. Beat: compassion reframing monsters as victims.

chapters.title: The Third Verse Refused
chapters.summary: The song offers Rafael the third verse as mercy—forget everything, join gently. She refuses aloud, and the annex shudders. POV: Rafael. Beat: agency asserted inside the trap.

chapters.title: What Love Costs
chapters.summary: In a vision, Rafael sees the life she could keep if she sings: warmth, tenure, Idris returned. The song negotiates. POV: Rafael. Beat: temptation crystallized; duty versus desire given a literal voice.

chapters.title: Idris Found
chapters.summary: Villagers find Idris alive at the treeline, remembering nothing, and the council declares the matter closed. Rafael, still missing, watches through a mirror. POV: Idris briefly, then Rafael. Beat: bittersweet rescue; the machine resets smoothly.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Overheard
chapters.summary: Trapped in the annex, Rafael hears the fourth verse sung by thirty voices including, horribly, her own future voice. She now knows it completely. POV: Rafael. Beat: point of no return—knowledge cannot be returned.

chapters.title: Aldous's Last Night
chapters.summary: Back in the village, Aldous dies peacefully with frost writing her name on her window—the ledger collects its oldest debtor. POV: Rafael via mirror-vision. Beat: consequences arrive for the complicit; justice outside the law.

chapters.title: Hale Comes to the Annex
chapters.summary: Hale, broken by guilt, enters the annex to take Rafael's place, but the song rejects him—it wants willing voices, and his is too afraid. POV: Rafael. Beat: tragedy of the enabler; fear disqualifies sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: Rafael understands the mechanism: the song persists because every voice sang to survive. To end it, someone must learn the last verse and give it away freely—not sing it, surrender it. POV: Rafael. Beat: thesis stated; the price of survival inverted.

chapters.title: Saying Goodbye
chapters.summary: Through every mirror in Hollowmere, Rafael says goodbye to Idris, who alone seems to half-hear her, and asks him to teach the class in spring. POV: Rafael. Beat: love against duty resolved into tenderness before the climax.

chapters.title: Solstice
chapters.summary: On solstice night Rafael stands before the blackboard and offers the last verse back to the frost—not sung but surrendered, note by note, as the village below sings the first three. POV: Rafael. Beat: climax; the song begins to unravel.

chapters.title: The Unmaking
chapters.summary: The taken children take up the surrendering verse, passing it hand to hand until the frost notation burns off the windows and the annex grows cold and ordinary. POV: Rafael. Beat: catharsis; thirty voices choosing an end together.

chapters.title: Spring Term
chapters.summary: Rafael returns voiceless to Hollowmere, where the extra desks have finally been removed and Idris keeps her promise. The mirrors reflect exactly on time. POV: Rafael. Beat: quiet resolution; survival redefined as what you give up, not what you keep.

chapters.title: The Song's Silence
chapters.summary: Final chapter: Rafael writes on the classroom board, 'We will remember them out loud,' and leads the class in a new song—one the frost has never heard. POV: Rafael. Beat: hope earned; the winter ends because someone finally paid a different price.
